First, let's recall the following result:

$$
\int {e}^{px+q}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{p}{e}^{px+q}+C
$$

We proceed by setting the upper bound equal to some parameter $a,$ integrating as usual, and then taking the limit as $a\to \infty .$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }2{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & ={lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}2{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{\int }_{0}^{a}{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[-\frac{1}{3}{e}^{-3x}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {lim}_{a\to \infty }{[{e}^{-3x}]}_{0}^{a} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{3a}}-1)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall the end behavior of the function $y=\frac{1}{{e}^{3x}},$ shown in the graph below:

- ${lim}_{x\to -\infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{3x}}=\infty $

- ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{3x}}=0$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14042659/assets/45e8ddd8ddb33dc8d6a701ed75878271b331ce6b3591ba8fae9f4fa49020c12b.png)

Using this to evaluate our integral, we conclude that

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{\infty }2{e}^{-3x}\,\text{d}x & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot ({lim}_{a\to \infty }\frac{1}{{e}^{3a}}-1) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}\cdot (0-1) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
